Living Unit Timeline • Part 1: Romans to Stuarts (c.43 AD–1665)

Pages 2–3 Facing Spread
How to use this timeline: As you study each lesson, illustrate the milestone sketchpad with your visual symbol and key notes. Spine • Facing Left
c.43–410 AD • Roman Aqueducts, Bathhouses & Fishbourne Lead Pipes Lesson 1

Roman engineers bring stone aqueducts, communal bathhouses, and gravity sewers to Britain. At Fishbourne Palace in Sussex, jointed lead water pipes carry fresh running water into garden pools and private bath suites, though ordinary Britons still rely on muddy streams.

Sketch your visual symbol: The stone arches of a Roman aqueduct or jointed lead pipes stamped with the imperial mark.
c.1100–1350 • Monastic Waterworks vs Medieval Town Squalor Lesson 2

While medieval towns choke on overflowing cesspits and hire night-time gong farmers, wealthy monasteries build clean water networks. Canterbury monks filter fresh spring water through five settling tanks into washing fountains and flush their infirmary latrines into the river.

Sketch your visual symbol: Monastic settling tanks or a gong farmer carrying barrels of waste at night.
1596–1665 • Tudor Flush Toilets & The 1665 Great Plague Lesson 3

Sir John Harington invents the flushing water closet in 1596, but without piped water it fails to catch on. When the Great Plague strikes in 1665, authorities lock families behind red crosses and plague doctors wear herb-filled beaks to ward off deadly miasma.

Sketch your visual symbol: The plague doctor’s long-beaked mask or the red cross with ‘Lord Have Mercy Upon Us’.
Timeline Check: Why did clean water systems collapse when the Romans left Britain, and why were monasteries able to stay so much cleaner than medieval towns? Turn overleaf for Lesson 1 →
2/16 "A Roman bath was not just for washing—it was where politics, deals, and gossip happened."

Living Unit Timeline • Part 2: Industrial Revolution & Modern Health (1842–1875)

Pages 2–3 Facing Spread
How to use this timeline: As you study each lesson, illustrate the milestone sketchpad with your visual symbol and key notes. Spine • Facing Right
1842–1848 • Chadwick’s Sanitary Report & The 1848 Health Act Lesson 4

Industrial cities grow into death traps of back-to-back terraces and cellar dwellings. Edwin Chadwick’s 1842 Report uses mortality statistics to prove filth causes early death, but the 1848 Public Health Act fails because it is voluntary and ratepayers resist taxes.

Sketch your visual symbol: Chadwick’s mortality scales (Rutland 38 vs Manchester 17) or slum houses.
1854 • Dr John Snow & The Broad Street Water Pump Lesson 5

Dr John Snow investigates a sudden cholera outbreak in Soho. By plotting deaths on a street map and discovering that brewery workers were spared, he proves cholera is water-borne and persuades parish officials to remove the Broad Street pump handle.

Sketch your visual symbol: The iron Broad Street pump with its handle removed, or the Soho spot map.
1858–1875 • The Great Stink & Bazalgette’s Underground Sewers Lesson 6

The blazing heat of June 1858 turns the Thames into a toxic sewer, forcing MPs to act. Joseph Bazalgette builds 82 miles of underground brick sewers. In 1875, the Public Health Act finally makes clean water and sanitation compulsory by law.

Sketch your visual symbol: Bazalgette’s egg-shaped brick sewer or the 1875 Public Health Act scroll.
Timeline Check: Which was the bigger breakthrough in conquering water-borne disease: Dr John Snow proving the cause in 1854, or Bazalgette building the sewers in 1858? Use for revision →
"Clean water is not an accident of nature; it is a triumph of engineering and public health." 3/16

Task 4: Source Utility • How useful are Sources A and B for an enquiry into how 17th-century London fought the Great Plague of 1665?

Source Utility
Source A: The Lord Mayor’s London Plague Orders (1665)

“Every visited house shall be shut up with a red cross marked upon the middle of the door, with these words: ‘LORD HAVE MERCY UPON US.’ A watchman shall stand day and night before the door, to keep the people from coming forth. All dogs and cats shall immediately be killed.”

Record: LONDON METROPOLITAN ARCHIVES • 1665 GUILDHALL PAPERS
Year 7 Clue: Official government rules showing how the city tried to quarantine sick families by force.
Source B: Dr Nathaniel Hodges, Eyewitness Doctor in London (1665)

“The shut-up houses became living graves. We wore long leather robes and beaks stuffed with sweet herbs to ward off the foul miasma in the air, yet still the pestilence devoured whole streets. Killing the dogs and cats was madness, for the black rats multiplied without check.”

Record: ROYAL COLLEGE OF PHYSICIANS • LOIMOLOGIA (1672)
Year 7 Clue: Eyewitness diary from a real doctor proving they believed in miasma and did not understand fleas and germs.
Planning Your Utility Answer: 3 Steps Draft quick bullet points below ↓
1. WHAT THE SOURCES SHOW What actions did the Lord Mayor and doctors take in 1665 (quarantine, red crosses, beak masks)?
2. WHO WROTE THEM & WHY Compare the official government orders to an eyewitness doctor's diary.
3. HOW USEFUL ARE THEY? How do both sources prove that 17th-century people did not understand bacteria and fleas?
Key Words: Plague Doctor • Red Cross • Quarantine • Dr Hodges • Lord Mayor Orders • Miasma • Black Rats • Watchmen
Sentence Starters: Source A is useful for showing that London authorities used quarantine because... • However, it only shows the official rules, not whether people obeyed them. • In contrast, Source B is useful because Dr Hodges was an eyewitness who saw... • Together, both sources are valuable because they prove...
[C] Content: What factual details does the source give? [P] Provenance: Who wrote it, when, and why? [K] Knowledge: Own facts about this event. [U] Utility: How useful is it for our enquiry?
Timeline Mission • Pages 2–3
Turn to Pages 2–3 (Milestone 3: 1596–1665). In the sketchpad, draw the plague doctor’s long-beaked mask or the red cross with ‘Lord Have Mercy Upon Us’.
"When assessing source utility, always ask: what does it reveal, who created it, and what are its limits?" 9/16

Task 3: Source Investigation — Dr John Snow’s Broad Street Cholera Spot Map (1854) Primary Evidence
Primary Cartography: Dr John Snow’s 1854 Spot Map of Soho

“Within 250 yards of the Broad Street pump, 500 deaths occurred in ten days. Nearby, at the Lion Brewery, none of the 70 workers died—they were given free beer and never drank pump water. At the workhouse with its own deep well, only 5 of 535 inmates caught cholera. On 7 September 1854, the pump handle was removed.”

Record: WELLCOME HISTORICAL MEDICAL COLLECTION • SNOW MONOGRAPH (1855)
Reading Clues:
① Underline: what happened to the 70 workers at the Lion Brewery.
② Circle: the date the Broad Street pump handle was removed (7 September 1854).
③ Box: the number of deaths within 250 yards of the pump (500 deaths).
Question 1: Why were the brewery workers and workhouse inmates the vital clues that solved the mystery?
Question 2: Why did doctors continue to believe in miasma for thirty years after Snow removed the pump handle?
Helpful Clue: Brewery workers drank boiled beer; workhouse inmates had their own private deep well. If bad smells in the air caused cholera, everyone would have died! Challenge Question: How did John Snow’s map create the modern science of epidemiology (tracking disease outbreaks)?
12/16 "John Snow mapped cholera deaths bar by bar to prove the water was poisoning Soho."
Unit: Water & Sanitation • Lesson 5 • Focus: Source Utility

Task 4: Source Utility • How useful are Sources A and B for an enquiry into whether Victorians believed cholera was caused by water or bad air (miasma)?

Source Utility
Source A: Dr John Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera (1855)

“Within 250 yards of the Broad Street pump, 500 fatal attacks occurred in 10 days. Yet in the Lion Brewery in Broad Street, where 70 workmen were employed, not one died of cholera. Mr Huggins informed me that the men were allowed free beer and never drank pump water. At the Eley factory, workers drank water carried from Broad Street—and scores died.”

Record: WELLCOME HISTORICAL MEDICAL COLLECTION • SNOW REPORT (1855)
Year 7 Clue: Scientific detective proof comparing beer drinkers and pump water drinkers to pinpoint the contaminated well.
Source B: General Board of Health Official Report on Cholera (1854)

“We see no reason to adopt Dr Snow’s belief that cholera is propagated through drinking water. The disease is caused by poisonous exhalations rising from decomposing filth and foul drains in overcrowded lanes. The impure atmosphere, especially in warm summer nights, poisons the blood of those breathing it.”

Record: BRITISH PARLIAMENTARY PAPERS • REPORT ON CHOLERA OUTBREAK
Year 7 Clue: Official government report proving top Victorian doctors stubbornly defended miasma theory despite Snow’s proof.
Planning Your Utility Answer: 3 Steps Draft quick bullet points below ↓
1. WHAT THE SOURCES SHOW Contrast Snow’s evidence (brewery workers spared vs factory workers dead) with the Board’s miasma claims.
2. WHO WROTE THEM & WHY Compare Snow’s door-to-door scientific investigation with the Board of Health defending traditional medical beliefs.
3. HOW USEFUL ARE THEY? How do both sources prove that even with solid evidence, Victorians struggled to abandon miasma theory?
Key Words: Dr John Snow • Broad Street pump • Lion Brewery • General Board of Health • Miasma Theory • Water-Borne • Contaminated well • Epidemiology
Sentence Starters: Source A is highly useful for proving that cholera was water-borne because Dr Snow discovered... • However, Source A does not explain why other doctors doubted him. • In contrast, Source B is useful because the Board of Health reveals that authorities still believed... • Together, both sources are valuable because they show that scientific breakthroughs...
[C] Content: What factual details does the source give? [P] Provenance: Who wrote it, when, and why? [K] Knowledge: Own facts about this event. [U] Utility: How useful is it for our enquiry?

Task 2: Key Vocabulary Core Definitions
Explain the difference between an Intercepting Sewer (a giant pipe that catches sewage before it hits the river and carries it far away) and Compulsory Legislation (a law that forces councils to build clean water systems):
Task 3: Source Investigation — Building Joseph Bazalgette’s Brick Sewers (c.1860s) Primary Evidence
Engineering Archive Plate: Construction of Egg-Shaped Brick Sewers Beneath London

“In June 1858, a blazing heatwave turned the River Thames into a bubbling stew of human waste. In the House of Commons, MPs fled the library holding scented handkerchiefs, and committee rooms were soaked in chloride of lime. Within 18 days, Parliament abandoned fifty years of excuses, passing a bill granting £3 million for Chief Engineer Joseph Bazalgette to build 82 miles of intercepting brick sewers.”

Record: INSTITUTION OF CIVIL ENGINEERS • BAZALGETTE PAPERS (1860)
Reading Clues:
① Underline: what MPs held over their faces when trying to work in Parliament.
② Circle: the number of days it took Parliament to pass the sewer law (18 days).
③ Box: the total length of underground intercepting brick sewers (82 miles).
Question 1: What does this source reveal about why politicians finally acted after ignoring slums for fifty years?
Question 2: How did Bazalgette’s egg-shaped sewers and Portland cement permanently wipe out cholera in London?
Helpful Clue: For decades, poor children died in cellars and MPs said taxes were too high. When MPs themselves couldn’t breathe in their own debating chamber, money was approved in 18 days! Challenge Question: How did Bazalgette’s sewers pave the way for the 1875 Public Health Act, making clean water a legal right in Britain?
14/16 "It took the Great Stink of 1858 boiling in Parliament to finally end fifty years of excuses."

[P] Point: Clear sentence answering the question. [E] Evidence: Names, dates, places, and statistics. [E] Explain: How and why this affected public health. [L] Link: Direct conclusion answering enquiry.

🎯 Summer Assessment Revision Protocol • 4 Evidence-Based Retrieval Techniques Cognitive Science in Practice
1. Spaced Flash Quizzing Scan each QR code weekly. Retest until you score 100% on factual recall before checking your workbook notes.
2. Dual-Coding Timeline Walk Turn to Pages 2–3. Cover the written text and narrate the historical story aloud using only your sketchpad symbols.
3. 5-Minute Brain Dumps Pick an enquiry question. Spend 5 uninterrupted minutes writing every name, date, and cause from memory.
4. Causal Connective Drills Draft 3 PEEL sentences explaining why an event happened using: Consequently... This directly resulted in...
